The Tyne Stop Line was an anti-tank defence line built in the north east of England during World War II to protect against a possible German invasion.
The line ran from the mouth of the River Tyne at Tynemouth, south to the River Wansbeck at Morpeth.
The line was designed to be defended by regular army units, with support from local Home Guard units.
The line was built as part of a wider network of stop lines across the country, which were intended to slow down any German advance and allow time for reinforcements to be brought up.
The Tyne Stop Line was never tested in combat, as the German invasion never materialised.

The Byzantines used subsidies as a diplomatic weapon of war in several ways.
One example is the payment of tribute to the Bulgarian Khan Tervel in the early 8th century.
The Byzantine emperor Justinian II had been deposed in a coup in 695 and had fled to the court of Tervel, who agreed to help him regain his throne in exchange for a large payment of gold.
Justinian II returned to Constantinople in 705 and resumed his reign, but he was unable to fulfill his promise to Tervel.
In response, Tervel invaded Byzantine territory and defeated the Byzantine army in battle.
Justinian II was forced to agree to pay Tervel an annual tribute of gold in exchange for peace.
This tribute continued to be paid by the Byzantine Empire for many years, and it helped to maintain a fragile peace between the two powers.
By using subsidies in this way, the Byzantines were able to avoid a costly and potentially disastrous war with the Bulgarians.
